summary: Robust Header Compression (ROHC) shrinks packet headers on links where bandwidth is precious. The profiles in RFC 3095 assume the link never reorders packets. This memo discusses what changes when the channel can reorder packets, gives guidance for running the existing profiles over such channels, and offers suggestions for designing new profiles.

plainLanguage.summary: ROHC compresses the repeated headers in a packet stream so that less bandwidth is needed. It assumes packets reach the decompressor in the order they were sent. This document explains how ROHC can still be used on links that shuffle packets, and why the claim that it cannot is a misunderstanding.

subtitle: How header compression built for in-order links can still be used on links that deliver packets out of order.

tldr.problem: The ROHC profiles assume the link between compressor and decompressor delivers packets in order, and ROHC has been faulted for that assumption on links that do not.
tldr.mechanism: The document analyses how reordering breaks each ROHC mode, then shows how a compressor or decompressor can be changed, and how a profile's sequence number window can be redefined, so that the existing profiles work over reordering channels.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational guidance document rather than a specification. It shows the claim that ROHC cannot cope with reordering is a misreading of RFC 3095, at the cost of some compression efficiency.

today: RFC 4224 is an Informational document from January 2006 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It describes how the ROHC profiles of RFC 3095 can be used over channels that reorder packets, and it is guidance for implementers and profile designers rather than a specification of new technology.

sections.title: The Assumption That Breaks
sections.content:
RObust Header Compression (ROHC), defined in RFC 3095, is a framework for header compression together with a number of compression protocols, called profiles. One operating assumption of those profiles is that the channel between compressor and decompressor is required to maintain packet ordering for each compressed flow. The assumption was reasonable when ROHC was designed, because the candidate channels considered did guarantee in-order delivery of header-compressed packets, and relying on it made it possible to meet the design objectives that were top of the requirements list at the time, namely better compression efficiency and tolerance to packet loss.

Since RFC 3095 was published in 2001 the question of running ROHC over channels that do not guarantee in-order delivery has surfaced several times, and arguments that ROHC cannot perform adequately over such channels have been heard, as a weakness compared with other header compression alternatives. The authors call this a misconception that is easy to understand given the wording of RFC 3095. This document explains different ways of implementing the profiles of RFC 3095, and profiles based on them, over reordering channels: either by ensuring the compressor uses compressed headers that are sufficiently robust to the expected reordering, or by modifying the decompressor to tolerate reordered packets. It also discusses how existing profiles could be updated and how new profiles could be defined to cope efficiently with reordering.

The document is informative and specifies no new technology. It also leaves aside the case where something outside ROHC, such as a sequence number, can already detect and possibly correct the reordering, which happens for example when compression runs over an IPsec Encapsulating Security Payload tunnel.
sections.plainLanguage: ROHC compresses the repeated headers in a packet stream so that less bandwidth is needed. It assumes packets reach the decompressor in the order they were sent. This document explains how ROHC can still be used on links that shuffle packets, and why the claim that it cannot is a misunderstanding.

sections.title: Terms for a Channel That Shuffles Packets
sections.content:
The document uses the terminology of RFC 3759 and adds the terms it needs. A reordering channel is a connection over which in-order delivery of header-compressed packets is not guaranteed. The candidate channels are single-hop channels, which are point-to-point links forming a single IP hop and possibly made up of one or more physical links, such as a wireless link that detects errors and retransmits, or a wireless connection that broadcasts data during a handoff. The other kind is a multi-hop virtual channel, typically an IP tunnel, where the endpoints of the tunnel apply compression to the tunnel itself.

A sequentially early packet reaches the decompressor before one or several packets of the same context identifier that were delayed on the link. At the moment it arrives, the delayed packets cannot be told apart from lost ones. A sequentially late packet is late within its sequence because it reaches the decompressor after one or several other packets of the same context identifier have been received, although it was sent from the compressor before them.

Not all packets behave the same way. An updating packet updates the context of the decompressor; in RFC 3095 all packet types except R-0 and R-1* do this. A non-updating packet does not update the context, and only R-0 and R-1* are of that kind. A change packet updates one or more fields of the context other than the fields that pertain to the sequence number: it updates fields other than the SN, the IPv4 identifier, the sequence number of an extension header, or the RTP timestamp.
sections.plainLanguage: A packet that arrives early looks exactly like a packet that was lost, because the receiver cannot tell the difference at first. A packet that arrives late was sent before packets the receiver already has. These two cases need different handling.

sections.title: How ROHC Keeps the Two Ends in Step
sections.content:
ROHC is based on the optimistic approach in the unidirectional and optimistic modes of operation, and on the secure reference principle in the bidirectional reliable mode. In the optimistic approach the compressor reduces header overhead when performing context updates by normally repeating the same update until it is fairly confident the decompressor has successfully received the information. The number of consecutive packets needed to obtain that confidence is open to implementations, and is normally related to the packet loss characteristics of the link where the compression is used. All packet types used in U/O-mode are context updating.

In the secure reference principle the compressor obtains its confidence that the decompressor has successfully updated the context from a packet carrying a 7- or 8-bit Cyclic Redundancy Check, based on the acknowledgements received from the decompressor. That confidence is what makes it possible for the compressor to use packets that do not update the context, R-0 and R-1*.

The two approaches have different characteristics in the presence of reordering between compressor and decompressor. They share one property: in any mode, decompression of sequentially early packets will generally be handled quite well, because the decompressor perceives them and treats them as if there had been one or more packet losses.
sections.plainLanguage: ROHC has two ways of keeping the sending and receiving ends in agreement. In the optimistic mode the sender repeats an update until it is confident the update arrived. In the reliable mode the receiver acknowledges what it got, and the sender only builds on references the receiver has confirmed. Reordering affects these two modes differently.

sections.title: How Far a Packet Can Move and Still Be Decompressed
sections.content:
The least significant bit encoding method of RFC 3095 places the sequence number inside an interpretation interval around a reference value, with an offset called p on the negative side. For profiles 0x0001, 0x0003 and 0x0007 the offset is p = 1 when the sequence number is at most 4 bits wide, and p = 2^(bits(SN)-5) - 1 otherwise. For profiles 0x0002, 0x0004 and 0x0008 the offset is always p = -1, independently of the size of the sequence number.

The negative offset is what decides how much reordering can be handled, because it is the largest amount by which the sequence number may differ from the reference and still be decompressed. With 8 bits of sequence number the offset is 7, so a packet that arrives up to 7 sequence numbers out of step can still be decompressed. With p = -1 no sequentially late packet can be decompressed at all, which is why the document calls out profiles 0x0002, 0x0004 and 0x0008 as needing special treatment: for them the sequence number is generated at the compressor, so it must increase for each packet received at the decompressor and reordered packets cannot be decompressed.

Adjusting p is a trade-off. The interpretation interval has size 2^k. Its lower bound is the reference minus p, which limits the reordering that can be handled, and its upper bound is the reference plus (2^k-1) - p, which limits the number of consecutive losses that can be handled. Raising p to cope with more reordering takes that room away from the loss side, and that may reduce compression efficiency when the channel has a high loss rate.
sections.plainLanguage: ROHC puts each sequence number inside a window of possible values around a reference. The size of the window on the low side, called p, decides how far a packet can arrive out of order and still be decoded. Making that side bigger helps with reordering but leaves less room for the decoder to survive lost packets.

sections.title: What Goes Wrong When Packets Arrive Out of Order
sections.content:
The document lists four effects of reordering. Some functionality cannot work. The ROHC segmentation scheme relies entirely on the in-order delivery of each segment, because the segments carry no sequencing information, so a segmented packet for which one or more segments arrive out of order cannot be decompressed and is discarded by the decompressor. Segmentation should therefore not be used if there can be reordering between the ROHC peers.

Context damage, that is a loss of synchronisation between the two ends, becomes more likely. The successful decompression of a sequentially late change packet in U/O-mode, or of a sequentially late updating packet in R-mode, can update the context of the decompressor in a manner unexpected by the compressor, and the peers lose synchronisation.

Some decompression failures are detected. For updating packets the outcome of the decompression can be verified, so the decompressor can reliably detect decompression failures, including those caused by reordering, and discard the packet.

Some failures are not detected, and this happens only in R-mode. The decompression of R-0 and R-1* packets cannot be verified. If reordering causes decompression to use the wrong secure reference, the decompressor cannot reliably detect the error, and erroneous packets may be forwarded to the upper layers. Two mechanisms produce this. The first is the missing reference: a sequentially late updating packet sets the decompressor reference to a value that is no longer in the sliding window of the compressor, so when the decompressor acknowledges it the compressor may already have discarded that reference and continue compressing against more recent ones, and later packets are decompressed against the wrong reference. The second is a non-updating packet that becomes sequentially late with respect to an updating packet, in which case the context has already been updated when the late packet is received.
sections.plainLanguage: Reordering breaks ROHC in four ways. Some features stop working, the two ends can fall out of step, and some packets fail to decompress. Most failures are caught, because updating packets carry a check. The dangerous case is the reliable mode, where non-updating packets cannot be checked, so a wrongly decoded packet can be passed on.

sections.title: Making ROHC Tolerate Reordering
sections.content:
Two groups of remedies are given. The first changes implementations rather than the protocol, and can be done without impairing interoperability with other ROHC implementations that do not use the methods. These methods may lower the compression efficiency, and they should not be used when reordering is known not to occur.

On the compressor side, the optimistic approach strategy should be adjusted to match both the packet loss and the reordering characteristics of the channel, for example by increasing the number of repetitions for each context update, so that each update is repeated until the compressor is reasonably confident that at least one change packet in the sequence has reached the decompressor before the first packet sent after that sequence. For the secure reference principle, the compressor can delay the advance of its sliding window to a reference that the decompressor has acknowledged, until it is confident that no acknowledgement for any of the values it could discard can still be received, a confidence it can base on the maximum delay that reordering can introduce over the channel.

The compressor can also select packet types conservatively, transmitting more sequence number bits, which provides larger negative offsets and so lets the decompressor handle more reordering. A compressor built this way always sends at least 3 octets in R-mode or 4 octets in U/O-mode, against the 1 octet that an aggressive implementation can send on a channel with no reordering.

On the decompressor side, feedback that arrives out of order causes no problem, but the decompressor should not send acknowledging feedback for a packet it can identify as sequentially late, because the current state of the context reflects the compressor better than the content of the reordered packet does. When decompression fails and reordering can be assumed to be the cause, the decompressor can retry by going backward in the interpretation interval rather than moving forward as in local repair, and pass the packet on if a retry succeeds. The decompressor should also reduce its feedback rate when the flow behaves linearly, so that a conservative compressor does not cause more feedback traffic on the link.

The second group of remedies changes the profile specification. New revisions of profiles 0x0002, 0x0004 and 0x0008 should redefine how the value of p is determined and use the same algorithm as profile 0x0001, instead of always using p = -1. Such a change would make those profiles slightly less robust to packet losses, but no less robust than profile 0x0001. For a profile meant to handle reordering, the document offers an example in which the positive range is about twice as large as the negative range, which leaves p = 2^k / 3, with values of 5, 10, 21, 42, 85 and 170 for 4 to 9 bits of sequence number. If a profile should be equally robust to reordering and to losses, p can be set near 2^k / 2.
sections.plainLanguage: The fix has two sides. An implementation can repeat updates, send more sequence number bits, hold back references and check for late packets, and none of that needs a change to the protocol. A profile can also be redefined so that its window allows more reordering, at the cost of tolerating fewer losses.

viz.caption: THE TWO ROBUSTNESS PRINCIPLES ROHC IS BUILT ON

items.title: Optimistic approach (U/O-mode)
items.text: The compressor repeats the same context update until it is fairly confident the decompressor received it. Every packet type used in this mode updates the context.

items.title: Secure reference principle (R-mode)
items.text: The compressor takes its confidence from a 7- or 8-bit checksum carried in acknowledgements, and may then use packets that do not update the context, R-0 and R-1*.

items.title: Sequentially early packets
items.text: Handled well in either mode, because the decompressor treats a packet that arrives early as if one or more packets had been lost.
